card.title: Designing A New Experience For Change Seekers
card.description: A ground-up rebuild of Wegovy.com — shifting a clinical pharma site toward a consumer-centered lifestyle journey. I directed UX strategy, content architecture, and an AI-architected wayfinding quiz with 45 unique outcome combinations.

hero.title: Wegovy
hero.subtitle: Designing A New Experience For Change Seekers

paragraphs: I led the ground-up rebuild of Wegovy.com, directing UX strategy, content architecture, and client relationships across a five-month engagement. Working alongside a UI Director, content strategists, and copywriters, I owned the experience vision from kickoff through launch — facilitating workshops, leading wireframe development, and serving as the primary point of contact for stakeholder communication and developer support during the AEM build.
This project also marked a milestone in how I leverage AI as a design tool, using ChatGPT, Claude, and Figma Make to architect a wayfinding quiz with 45 unique outcome combinations.

cards.label: 01 — Accessibility
cards.title: A site that couldn't be used by everyone
cards.body: Text in images. Insufficient contrast. Compliance failures at nearly every level. The site couldn't meet WCAG standards — a critical failure for a healthcare product in a regulated space.

cards.label: 02 — Experience
cards.title: Clinical documentation framed as a consumer journey
cards.body: Wegovy is a lifestyle product. The site read like a pharmaceutical package insert. The architecture, tone, and visual design all prioritized compliance over connection — leaving real patients without a clear path forward.

sections.heading:
Organizing around
the patient journey.
sections.body: We replaced a compliance-first architecture with a four-stage consumer journey — built around the questions real patients actually ask, in the order they ask them.

stages.title: Is Wegovy Right for Me
stages.subtitle: Education and eligibility — meeting patients before they've decided.

stages.title: How Do I Get It
stages.subtitle: Prescription pathways explained clearly, without clinical jargon.

stages.title: What Will I Pay
stages.subtitle: Cost, insurance, and savings programs — the questions that kill conversion.

stages.title: Getting Started
stages.subtitle: Onboarding and expectations — setting patients up for success after they've decided.

sections.heading:
Five questions.
45 unique outcomes.
bodyTexts: The quiz was the most technically complex piece of the project — and the most human. The challenge wasn't writing five questions. It was ensuring every combination of answers led somewhere meaningful, not a dead end or a generic page.

I used AI (ChatGPT and Claude) to architect the full decision tree — mapping all possible answer combinations to appropriate outcome CTAs. What would have taken weeks of spreadsheet logic took days. Figma Make handled the prototype, letting us test real paths with stakeholders before a line of AEM code was written.
sections.pullquote: AI didn't replace the thinking — it accelerated it.

details.heading: How It Was Built
details.body: Decision tree architecture built collaboratively with AI. Every path validated against user journey stages. Prototype in Figma Make for stakeholder review before a single line of AEM code was written.

details.heading: Client Reaction
details.body: Overwhelmingly positive. The quiz became one of the defining features of the new site — a tangible example of AI as a design tool, not a replacement for design thinking.

columns.title: Accessibility Leadership
items: WCAG-compliant architecture from day one
Eliminated all text-in-image patterns
Established contrast standards and focus states
Full keyboard navigation coverage
Structured for screen reader compatibility

columns.title: Design System
items: First implementation of new Novo Nordisk design system
Token-based architecture for cross-product scalability
Designed for reuse across Ozempic, Rybelsus, and future products
Brand-aligned while staying platform-consistent

columns.title: Partnership Model
items: Workshop-based alignment at kickoff and key milestones
Direct stakeholder access earned by mid-project
Collaborative MLR (medical-legal-regulatory) process
Primary AEM liaison through the full build phase

sections.heading: Shipped in five months.
list: NovoCare conversion and savings card signups as primary KPIs
Reduced bounce from misaligned entry page experiences
Accessible architecture built in, not retrofitted
Scalable token-based design system deployed
AI-powered wayfinding quiz live on site at launch
Experience quality tracked alongside conversion metrics

reflection.quote: This project represents the fullest expression of how I lead. I did IC work when IC work was needed. I led when leadership was needed. I knew which moments called for which.

card.title: Finding The 'Beef' In New, More Efficient Ways
card.description: A year embedded with Wendy's product team, redesigning their digital ordering experience from the ground up. Result: 70% fewer interactions to complete an order.

hero.title: Wendy's
hero.subtitle: Finding The 'Beef' In New, More Efficient Ways

paragraphs: As the sole design lead on Wendy's digital ordering squad, I spent a year embedded with the product and engineering teams focused on one mission: make ordering faster.

The competitive landscape demanded it. QSR value wars were intensifying. Competitors were shipping leaner flows. And our own data confirmed what we already suspected — too many taps, too many screens standing between a customer and their order.
The result: a 70% reduction in the interactions required to complete an order.

sections.heading:
One sentence that
set the standard.
sections.quote: I want to be able to order Wendy's at a red light.
bodyTexts: That one sentence did more to focus the work than any requirements document could. Every design decision had a test: could a driver complete this in the span of a red light? If not, something needed to change.

The stakes were concrete. Competitors were already shipping faster. User research confirmed the scale of the problem — 30+ interactions to complete a single order. But the path forward wasn't obvious, because not everyone agreed there was a problem.

sections.heading: Three pockets of change.
sections.body: The redesign wasn't a wholesale rebuild — it was surgical. We identified three distinct areas where friction compounded and engineered each one down independently.

pockets.title: Location
pockets.problem: Five decisions before users could even see a menu. New user setup was a maze. Returning users had to re-confirm everything they'd already told us.
pockets.solution: Defaulting logic built around recent preferences. Streamlined new user setup. Location intelligence that worked in the background, not in the way.

pockets.title: Menu
pockets.problem: Combo building required separate screens for every modification. Each customization felt like its own journey. The path from browsing to bag was never clear.
pockets.solution: Consolidated customization into a single scrollable interaction. Smarter defaults surfaced the most common modifications first. A shorter, cleaner path straight to bag.
pockets.impact: Dramatic reduction in interactions per item

pockets.title: Checkout
pockets.problem: The bag screen tried to do everything at once — order review, payment, pickup options, upsells, loyalty rewards. The result was a wall of decisions that caused errors and abandonment.
pockets.solution: Split into two purpose-built screens: order verification first, payment and logistics second. Each screen had one job. Users moved faster and made fewer mistakes.

sections.heading: Seventy percent.
bodyTexts: That's the headline. But the number only happened because every other thing fell into place first — the research, the trust, the engineering relationships, the stakeholder work. The design was almost the easy part.
sections.pullquote: 70% reduction is the headline. The real work was creating the conditions that made those changes possible.

details.heading: App Store Validation
details.body: The improvements were visible enough that users wrote about them. App Store reviews specifically called out the faster ordering experience — unprompted feedback that confirmed the reduction wasn't just measurable, it was felt.

details.heading: Design → Advocacy
details.body: The Director of Product, initially one of the harder relationships to navigate, became a genuine design advocate by the end of the engagement. That trust outlasted the project — and opened doors that design output alone never would have.

sections.heading: People problems.
bodyTexts: A significant portion of early research feedback insisted the app was fine. "Loyalists" — users who had adapted to every inefficiency — confused familiarity with quality. The key stakeholder on the original build fell into this camp too.
The solution wasn't better designs. It was better evidence. User data became the only currency that mattered.

columns.title: The Loyalist Problem
items: Power users had adapted to every inefficiency
Familiarity was being mistaken for usability
User research had to do the heavy lifting
Data — not opinion — was the only argument that landed
The resistant stakeholder was eventually won over by the numbers

columns.title: Stakeholder Navigation
items: Built trust with the Director of Product as executive advocate
Earned direct stakeholder access through demonstrated judgment
The relationships built mattered as much as the work shipped
Cross-functional credibility opened doors the work alone couldn't

columns.title: Engineering Partnership
items: Offshore team across multiple time zones
Deliberate relationship-building from day one
Platform migration to Flutter enabled a proper design system
Component library built for longevity, not just the next sprint
Designers stepped into leadership of ongoing initiatives

Taps to place
a complete order

reflection.quote: This project reinforced something I've come to believe strongly: the hardest problems in product design aren't design problems. They're people problems.
reflection.followUp: 70% is the headline. But the real work was building the trust, navigating the resistance, and creating the conditions that made those changes possible in the first place.

card.title: A Digital Presence Worthy of Its Legacy
card.description: End-to-end UX strategy for Virginia State University — modernizing a 2009-era digital experience while honoring the legacy of one of America's longest-running HBCUs.

hero.title:
Virginia State
University
hero.subtitle: A Digital Presence Worthy of Its Legacy

paragraphs: As UX Lead, I directed end-to-end research and design strategy for Virginia State University's digital transformation — a remote engagement conducted during COVID in 2020, partnering with a UX Architect to modernize one of the nation's longest-running HBCUs.
The scope was substantial: 100+ pages organized across six primary navigation trees, serving five distinct audience groups with fundamentally different needs and mental models.
The tools were Sketch, Craft, and InVision. The challenge was far larger than the toolset.

sections.heading:
A legacy institution.
A dated presence.
sections.body: Virginia State University holds a distinguished legacy as one of the nation's longest-running HBCUs. But in 2020, its web presence reflected a 2009-era experience — a gap that mattered more than ever in a competitive higher education landscape.

cards.label: 01 — The Gap
cards.title: Legacy institution, dated digital reality
cards.body: Higher education is a buyer's market. Prospective students evaluate institutions digitally before they ever set foot on campus. VSU was competing alongside peer HBCUs — Howard, Hampton, Spelman — with a site that couldn't tell its story or serve its community.

cards.label: 02 — The Mission
cards.title: Modernize without erasing the identity
cards.body: The goal wasn't just a visual refresh. It was rebuilding the digital ecosystem to serve a diverse audience, reinforce brand equity in a crowded landscape, and capture the spirit of campus life — all without sacrificing accessibility compliance.

sections.heading:
Five audiences.
One unified framework.
sections.body: Research began with a hypothesis-driven survey methodology across all five audience groups — each with different goals, different entry points, and different definitions of success on the site.

audiences.title: Current Students
audiences.note: Navigating academics, registration, campus resources. Efficiency above everything.

audiences.title: Prospective Students
audiences.note: Evaluating VSU against peer institutions. First impression is the only impression.

audiences.title: Parents
audiences.note: Seeking safety, cost, and outcomes information. Trust-building at every step.

audiences.title: Alumni
audiences.note: Giving, reconnecting, staying engaged. Emotional connection over utility.

audiences.title: Faculty & Staff
audiences.note: Administrative access, departmental visibility, institutional tools.

sections.pullquote: When debates arose about navigation priorities or content hierarchy, we could return to the personas and ask: "Who are we solving for here, and what do they actually need?"

details.heading: Personas as Decision Tools
details.body: The five personas weren't deliverables — they were instruments. They shaped every IA debate, every navigation tradeoff, every content priority. A persona that sits in a deck and never gets referenced again isn't a design tool. It's a document.

details.heading: The Unifying Insight
details.body: Despite their differences, all five audiences shared a single primary goal: find information efficiently. That shared need became the governing principle for every architectural decision that followed.

sections.heading:
100+ pages.
Three key decisions.
sections.body: A site of this scale can't be designed page by page. We moved to a template-based architecture — designing systems, not screens — and made three structural decisions that shaped everything else.

items.title: Mega-Navigation
items.body:
VSU's content hierarchy was genuinely complex — six primary navigation trees serving audiences with completely different needs. A conventional nav would bury content or force users into deep drilling.

The mega-nav surfaced secondary destinations at the top level, reducing cognitive load without hiding complexity.

items.title: Global Utility Header
items.body:
Analytics told us ~80% of homepage traffic had the same intent: find email, find directory, find portal. That intent was being sent into the main nav to compete with prospective student content.

The utility header gave returning users a dedicated lane — and freed the main nav to speak to new audiences.

items.title: College-Specific Navigation
items.body:
Each of VSU's colleges had its own identity, its own content needs, its own audiences. A fully centralized nav would erase that. Full autonomy would fracture the experience.

College-specific navigation instances preserved university-wide consistency while giving each college room to breathe.

sections.heading:
Built on evidence,
earned through process.

columns.title: Usability Validation
items: Moderated usability testing across all five persona groups
Users praised IA clarity across every segment
Navigation tested intuitive without prompting
Only minor visual refinements required after testing
Architecture validated before a single page was designed

columns.title: Stakeholder Navigation
items: Early sprint reviews met with silence — not agreement
Developed targeted discussion prompts to surface real feedback
Reframed decisions as tradeoffs, not recommendations
Built informal rapport alongside formal review cadence
Stakeholder alignment as critical as design quality

columns.title: 508 Accessibility
items: Third 508 engagement — first in higher education
Healthcare and financial services experiences applied to a new context
Campus atmosphere and emotional resonance retained within compliance
Accessibility treated as a design lens, not a compliance checklist
Decisions serving compliance almost always served clarity too

sections.heading: A dated maze, transformed.
list: Navigation tested intuitive across all persona groups
508 accessibility compliance achieved in higher ed for the first time
Template-based IA reduced design and dev overhead at scale
Stakeholder alignment achieved through process, not persuasion
Mega-nav reduced browsing depth for complex content hierarchy
Campus atmosphere preserved within accessibility constraints

reflection.quote: Accessibility isn't a compliance checkbox. It's a design lens. And every time we made a decision that served compliance, it almost always served clarity too.
reflection.followUp: This project also reinforced something about how I think about scale: strategic template systems outperform page-by-page design every time. And proactive stakeholder engagement isn't a soft skill — it's as critical as the design work itself.

card.title: Revitalizing Three Professional Tool Brands at Once
card.description: Led the simultaneous digital relaunch of three professional tool brands — Gearwrench, Crescent, and SATA — with distinct brand identities built on shared infrastructure.

hero.title: APEX Tools
hero.subtitle: Three brands. One platform. No compromises.

paragraphs: ACD on the simultaneous digital relaunch of three professional tool brands under the Apex Tool Group umbrella. Three distinct audiences — mechanics (Gearwrench), contractors and DIY (Crescent), industrial and body shop (SATA) — each with their own visual identity, their own content strategy, and their own expectations. One shared platform underneath all of it.
The challenge wasn't building three websites. It was building one system flexible enough to serve three entirely different product stories without collapsing into a generic middle ground.

sections.heading: Three layers. Infinite edge cases.
sections.body: The only way to make three-brand work viable was to be explicit about what lived at which layer. Every decision had to land somewhere. If the decision was wrong about where it belonged, it either broke something or slowed everything down.

pockets.title: Shared Infrastructure
pockets.solution: Common platform, checkout, account management, backend integrations. Users never see it. Every brand benefits from it. Non-negotiable.

pockets.title: Unified UX Patterns
pockets.solution: Navigation, product detail page layouts, filtering systems, mobile behaviors. Consistent enough to learn once. Flexible enough to feel brand-appropriate.

pockets.title: Brand-Specific Expression
pockets.solution: Visual identity, photography direction, copy tone, homepage storytelling. This is where Gearwrench looks nothing like SATA. Intentionally.

sections.heading: One platform. Three identities.
sections.body: Each brand served a different professional audience. Design decisions that worked for one didn't automatically work for the others — and that was the point. The system had to hold without flattening.

brands.name: Gearwrench
brands.description: Socket sets, wrenches, and drive tools for the shop floor. Dense product catalog. Users who know exactly what they need and need to find it fast.

brands.name: Crescent
brands.description: Hand tools spanning professional trades and weekend projects. Broader audience range with more educational content needs and a warmer, approachable tone.

brands.name: SATA Tools
brands.description: Spray guns and finishing equipment for body shop professionals. Highly specialized. Small, expert audience that needs depth over breadth.

sections.heading: E-commerce complexity at three scales.
bodyTexts: Each brand sat at the intersection of direct-to-consumer, retail partners, and industrial distributors — all within one coherent experience. Deep product catalogs demanded filtering by tool type, drive size, material, and application. And three brand teams, each with strong existing identities and legitimate opinions, meant the governance model mattered as much as the design.

columns.title: Channel Complexity
items: Direct-to-consumer, retail, and industrial distribution in one system
Channel-specific pricing and availability logic
Product data that had to work across wildly different catalog depths
Buy flows that respected how each audience actually purchases

columns.title: Catalog Architecture
items: Filtering systems across tool type, drive size, material, application
Product relationships (what fits what) as a navigation challenge
Technical spec depth for expert users without overwhelming new ones
Mobile-first product discovery for in-aisle and shop-floor use

columns.title: Brand Governance
items: Three brand teams, three visual identities, three sets of opinions
Brand teams own visual and content decisions
Platform decisions centralized and non-negotiable
Documented decision rights reduced conflict and accelerated delivery

sections.heading: Three brands. One delivery.
bodyTexts: Three simultaneous brand launches on a shared platform. The number sounds straightforward. The execution required constant navigation between brand-level advocacy and platform-level discipline — and knowing exactly which instinct to trust in each moment.
sections.pullquote: The right boundary between brand differentiation and platform standardization isn't a design decision. It's a leadership decision.

sections.heading: Platform thinking pays off.

stats.label:
Conversion rates
across all three sites

list: Time-to-product decreased across all three sites
Conversion rates improved post-launch
Post-launch research showed users perceived each brand's distinct value more clearly
Shared infrastructure reduced ongoing maintenance burden significantly
Governance model became the template for future brand acquisitions
Design system portable enough to onboard new brands without a rebuild

reflection.quote: Multi-brand work demands comfort with tension. Brand teams will always push for differentiation; platform teams will always push for standardization. Neither instinct is wrong — the skill is finding the right boundary between them.
reflection.followUp: On APEX, that boundary lived at the UX layer. Visual identity was entirely brand-owned. Interaction patterns were platform-owned. The moment we made that explicit — and stopped relitigating it in every design review — everything moved faster.

card.title: A Multi-Brand Digital Transformation
card.description: Five consumer brand relaunches under one engagement — Krylon, Cabot, Purdy, Thompson's Water Seal, and Minwax — each distinct in voice, unified in architecture.

hero.title: Sherwin-Williams
hero.subtitle: Five brands. One system. Infinite stakeholders.

paragraphs: The simultaneous digital relaunch of five consumer brand websites: Krylon, Cabot, Purdy, Thompson's Water Seal, and Minwax. Each brand had its own audience, its own visual identity, its own content strategy, and its own team with strong opinions about all three. One ACD responsible for the coherence of all of it.

Product discovery was broken across all five brands. Rich how-to content existed but was disconnected from the purchase journey. Mobile experiences lagged despite significant in-store mobile research behavior. And the digital presence, as it stood, was flattening the very brand differentiation Sherwin-Williams had spent decades building.

sections.heading: Same system. Five different stories.
sections.body: Each brand served a distinct audience with distinct content needs. The design system had to be consistent enough to maintain at scale and flexible enough that a Minwax user and a Krylon user never felt like they were on the same website.

brands.name: Krylon
brands.description: Spray paint for makers, crafters, and weekend projects. Bold, energetic tone. Users who want inspiration as much as product information.

brands.name: Cabot
brands.description: Stains and finishes for decks, fences, and wood surfaces. Craftsman aesthetic. A mix of serious DIY and professional applicators.

brands.name: Purdy
brands.description: Premium brushes and application tools. Heavy on bulk ordering and professional specifications. Users who already know exactly what they want.

brands.name: Thompson's Water Seal
brands.description: Waterproofing sealants with strong seasonal and regional demand. Simple product line with high educational content needs — the 'why' matters as much as the 'what.'

brands.name: Minwax
brands.description: Interior wood stains and finishes. Guided product selection by wood type and desired finish. Users who need help deciding, not just browsing.

bodyTexts: It would have been faster in the short term to build five independent sites. Each brand team gets exactly what they want. No negotiation. No governance overhead. Ship and move on.

But that approach leaves Sherwin-Williams with five separate codebases, five separate design systems, five separate maintenance burdens — and no ability to onboard a sixth brand without rebuilding everything from scratch. The system approach required more upfront investment and more coordination overhead. It also positioned the business for sustainable growth rather than accumulating technical debt with every new brand or feature request.

sections.heading: Four things broken across five brands.
sections.body: Before touching design, we needed to understand what was actually failing. User research across all five brands surfaced a consistent set of problems — different in severity by brand, identical in kind.

findings.title: 01 — Product Discovery
items: Search and browse broken across all five brands
Users couldn't filter by project type, surface, or finish
The "right product for my project" journey didn't exist
Guided selection tools present on zero of five sites at project start

findings.title: 02 — Content Disconnection
items: Rich how-to content existed but lived separately from products
No bridge between inspiration/education and purchase
Minwax and Cabot had deep project guides that went nowhere
Thompson's seasonal content wasn't tied to purchase timing

findings.title: 03 — Mobile Experience
items: In-store mobile research behavior was significant and unserved
Users consulting product pages in hardware aisles got a desktop experience
Mobile usability lagged significantly despite that use case being documented
No in-store mode, no quick comparison, no spec at a glance

findings.title: 04 — Brand Flattening
items: Despite distinct brand identities, sites felt like one generic template
Krylon and Purdy had nearly identical homepage structures
Visual differentiation that existed offline wasn't translating digitally
Brand teams were frustrated — the investment in brand wasn't showing up online

sections.heading: Five brands. One delivery.
bodyTexts: Five simultaneous brand launches. Different visual identities, different content strategies, different audiences. One underlying system flexible enough to serve them all distinctly — and scalable enough that a sixth brand could plug in without a rebuild.
sections.pullquote: Standardized: interaction patterns, navigation, product detail templates, accessibility, performance. Customized: typography, color, imagery, tone, feature prioritization. Those two lists never got mixed up.

sections.heading: Coordination at scale.
bodyTexts: Five brand teams. Five sets of priorities. One cross-functional process that had to hold. The design process was as much about tradeoff framing as it was about design output.

columns.title: Weekly Design Reviews
items: Cross-brand design reviews to maintain system coherence
Brand-specific reviews to protect identity decisions
Tradeoff framing: every "no" came with an alternative
Design system governance as a living document, not a one-time artifact

columns.title: Stakeholder Management
items: Bi-weekly syncs with five brand stakeholder groups
Sprint-based delivery with visible progress for each team
Competing priorities surfaced early, resolved before they became blockers
Executive-level communication for system-level decisions

columns.title: Technical Scalability
items: Shared component library maintained by a centralized team
Brand customization through tokens, not one-off overrides
Performance budgets applied system-wide, not brand-by-brand
Future acquisition onboarding built into the architecture from day one

sections.heading: Five brands. Better.
list: Guided product selection tools live on Minwax and Cabot at launch
How-to content woven into purchase journey on Thompson's and Krylon
Mobile usability significantly improved, in-store use case specifically designed for
Shared system established as the foundation for future brand acquisitions
Each brand team felt — and could demonstrate — distinct brand expression online
Post-launch research confirmed users perceived each brand's unique value more clearly

reflection.quote: What made this project distinct from single-brand work was the constant negotiation between system-level thinking and brand-level advocacy. Both are legitimate perspectives. Neither can win completely.
reflection.followUp: The work that matters most on a project like this rarely shows up in a portfolio screenshot. It shows up in the governance model. In the decision rights document. In the stakeholder relationship that made five simultaneous launches possible without five simultaneous fires.

card.title: I built this. All of it.
card.description: A meta case study about what happens when a design leader runs the full product lifecycle solo — from content strategy to deployed CMS — and what it changes about how you lead.

hero.title: I built this. All of it.
hero.subtitle: This case study is not about a website. It's about what happens when a design leader removes the walls between disciplines and runs the whole product lifecycle himself. The website is evidence. The process is the point.

sections.heading: A portfolio that was contradicting itself
sections.quote: Most designers outsource everything outside of design. This project was about closing those gaps.
bodyTexts: The surface problem: I needed a portfolio. The deeper problem: a static Squarespace site was actively contradicting the claim that I think in systems and ship things.
Every update required cloning a repo and manually editing code. For a site that needed to evolve as fast as a job search, that friction was a liability.
So this became two briefs. Build a portfolio that proves systems thinking. Then — post-launch — build the tools to keep it current without engineering overhead.

sections.heading: Content strategy before design
bodyTexts: Before a single pixel, a content audit. Most designers skip this step. It's a discipline problem, not a tool problem.

columns.title: The Audit
items: Scraped every page of the existing site
Catalogued every headline, tagline, and description
Tagged each line: validates the past, or claims the future?

columns.title: The Filter
items: One question: does this reflect a CD candidate?
Everything that answered no got cut
What remained was rewritten to close the gap

columns.title: The Output
items: A structured markdown brief
Single source of truth for design, engineering, and copy
Every subsequent decision traced back to it

sections.heading: Design system before site
sections.body: Tokens first, components second. One-sentence brief: near-black, amber-accented, editorial — typographically bold where it counts, sparse everywhere else.

findings.title: Color
items: Near-black (#0D0D0D) primary surface
Amber accent — 3–4 touches per viewport max
Warm authority, not loudness

findings.title: Typography
items: Roboto for display weight
DM Sans for body — readable and distinctive
Fluid scale via CSS clamp() — no breakpoint hacks

findings.title: Tokens
items: All spacing as CSS custom properties
Background variants: default, surface, surface-alt
System defined before pages, not extracted from them

findings.title: Reference + Divergence
items: Referenced editorial and design-forward portfolios
Diverged: less decoration, more typographic weight
Everything ornamental was a question, not a default

sections.heading: Engineering & first launch
bodyTexts: First launch shipped May 20. The design didn't stop at Figma — it went all the way to production.
This is where AI's role becomes explicit. Accelerant, not author. Every architectural decision was made by a human who understood the tradeoffs.

columns.title: Stack
items: Next.js 15 App Router
TypeScript
Custom CSS — full token control
Static generation via generateStaticParams

columns.title: Deployment
items: Vercel — auto-deploy on push to main
Zero manual steps after initial config
Custom domain, SSL, edge CDN

columns.title: AI's Role
items: Accelerant, not author
Architectural decisions made by a human
AI removed the parts that don't require judgment

cards.label: The Friction
cards.title: Every update required a commit
cards.body: Adding a project meant editing JSON files, running a local build, and pushing a commit. For a site evolving as fast as a job search, that's unacceptable.

cards.label: The Decision
cards.title: Build custom over adopt headless
cards.body: Sanity and Contentful solve the right problem — but add dependency, cost, and abstraction. This was solvable in-house. Building it was itself a proof point.

cards.label: The Scope
cards.title: Password-protected /admin with full CRUD
cards.body: JWT auth, protected routes, project editor with visual section builder, site content editor. One surface, no external services, no ongoing cost.

sections.heading: Four versions. One direction.
sections.body: Each version solved a specific problem. The direction never changed — only what was possible.

stages.title: Design + Launch
stages.subtitle: Content strategy, design system, full-stack build. Live on Vercel in ~2 weeks.

stages.title: Core CMS
stages.subtitle: JWT auth, project editor, site content editor. No code required to update the portfolio.

stages.title: Section Builder
stages.subtitle: 13 section components. Visual card-based editor. Case study page: 800 lines → 110.

stages.title: Production Persistence
stages.subtitle: GitHub API writes. Every save commits to the repo. Vercel rebuilds automatically.

paragraphs: The /admin interface handles the full content lifecycle without touching code.
Projects, sections, and site content are all editable from a single password-protected dashboard. Every save commits directly to the repo — no terminal, no deploy command, no engineering overhead.
sections.imageAlt: The /admin CMS dashboard — project list and visual section editor

sections.heading: By the numbers

stats.label: Lines on the case study page

list: Visual section builder — no schema knowledge required to author content
All case study content editable from /admin without touching code or a terminal
Every content save is a traceable, reversible git commit

sections.heading: Solving the production persistence problem
sections.body: Vercel’s serverless runtime has a read-only filesystem. The right fix depended on which tradeoffs were worth accepting.

findings.title: The Constraint
items: Vercel serverless functions can’t write to the filesystem
Every CMS save was silently failing with EROFS in production
Surfaced only after adding proper error handling to API routes

findings.title: Options Considered
items: Vercel KV: instant writes, but external dependency and no git history
GitHub API: 1–2 min rebuild, no external service, every save is a commit
Filesystem fallback: fine locally, not viable on Vercel

findings.title: The Decision
items: GitHub Contents API — chosen for simplicity and auditability
Fetch file SHA → commit updated JSON → Vercel detects push and rebuilds

reflection.quote: Running a full product lifecycle — including the parts that used to require handing off to someone else — changes how you lead a team.
reflection.followUp: You understand the real cost of a late design change. You know which engineering decisions are genuinely constrained and which are just habit. You write better briefs because you've been on the other end of bad ones. This project was built with Claude as a collaborator throughout — content strategy, design direction, every line of code. The judgment calls — what to cut, what to build, what tradeoff to make — were human. AI accelerated every phase by removing the parts that don't require judgment. That's the integration model, not the replacement model. The walls between disciplines are expensive. This project is proof that they're also optional.
